content.thinking:
I should use AL1 instead, and drop the duplicate second call since it was just a placeholder mistake. Let me double-check my action item numbering — existing items are AI-1 and AI-2, so mine should be AI-3 through AI-5: one-at-a-time rollout, revert order, and a guard note. That covers factor 1 via AI-3/AI-4, and factor 3 via AI-2.

Now I'm proofreading figures and references — the stack trace line "src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47" should stay verbatim since it's quoted from the log, but I'll soften other mentions of "line 47" to just "that line" to avoid stray digits in prose. Everything else, like "ZeroDivisionError" and "Argus picked up within seconds," reads fine as is.

action_items.item: Roll out flag changes to production one at a time, with a gap between them and a check of the error rate after each. Flags that change the same code path should not be toggled together.

When several flags changed in the same minute, have the mitigation step revert them in a defined order. It should weigh any flag named in the incident thread and test candidates one at a time with a short check, so a wrong first guess costs less time.

Add a guard or note on legacy-checkout-fallback saying that switching it off sends account pages to the new renderer. The note should say it must stay on until the spend-summary fix is merged and verified.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account pages fail. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average while broken, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. A large share of requests failed that otherwise would not have, and the HighErrorRate alert fired.
The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. The earlier ClientDisconnected errors were a different, baseline error.

Those requests ran the spend-summary code because legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off at the onset. That moved account pages from the legacy renderer, which had served them almost entirely, onto the new renderer. The new-renderer count rose from typically {Gc27d.10} to as high as {Gc27d.9}. Turning the flag back on stopped the incident, which confirms it. Ruled out: monthly-spend-feature was switched on in the same minute, but reverting it left the service at the incident's level. No deploy or release was recorded in the preceding day.

The new renderer's spend-summary code fails on ordinary input. Code-Fix's reading is that the failing line divides the month's total by this month's purchase count, which is zero for shoppers who bought before but not this month. This is a static reading of the source that nothing ran, so it is unverified. The record does not show why this path went out without handling that case.

contributing_factors.factor: Two feature flags were changed in the same minute, monthly-spend-feature on and legacy-checkout-fallback off. This made it hard to tell which one mattered, and the first revert targeted the wrong one.

The first mitigation reverted monthly-spend-feature, which the stack trace pointed at. The flag named in the thread and changed in the same minute was only tried after that revert was judged refuted, so the fix came later than it could have.
The new renderer's spend-summary path could not handle a shopper with no purchases this month. No test covering that case was seen in the record. Code-Fix has proposed one with its draft fix.
The mitigation is a flag revert, and the underlying defect is still in the new renderer until the fix is merged. Someone could switch the fallback off again.

input.executive_summary: Account pages on the shop failed for a share of shoppers for {duration}. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, against {errors_before} beforehand. An administrator had switched off a fallback setting that kept account pages on the older page renderer. Pages then moved to a newer renderer, which crashes for some shoppers. Argus first reverted a different setting that had changed in the same minute, and that did not help. It then turned the fallback setting back on, and the error rate returned to normal. A draft fix for the crash has been proposed and is awaiting review. Until it is merged, the fallback has to stay on.

lead_effects.effect: It did not change the order of actions, because the investigation ranked it second and tried monthly-spend-feature first. Once that was refuted, the flag the lead named was reverted and fixed the incident.

got_lucky: The previous flag state was still available to revert to, the legacy renderer served requests correctly, and the revert took effect quickly.
The record does not show why monthly-spend-feature's revert had no effect. If the two flags had interacted, reverting one at a time might not have worked.
went_well: The paging alert fired and Argus picked the incident up within seconds, after the paging rule's {rule_waits} wait.
Argus judged each revert against the metrics. It put the refuted revert back, tried the second candidate and confirmed it, and the rule that paged stopped firing.
Code-Fix produced a draft pull request with tests soon after mitigation.
went_wrong: The first revert targeted monthly-spend-feature and did not help, so the incident ran longer before the effective revert.
The thread lead naming the correct flag was weighed as unverified and ranked second. It was only acted on after the first action was refuted.
Two flag changes made by the same admin in the same minute left the cause ambiguous.

input.root_cause: Switching legacy-checkout-fallback off moved account pages from the legacy renderer onto the new renderer. The new renderer's spend-summary code raises ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py. Code-Fix's static reading, which nothing ran and which is unverified, is that it divides by this month's purchase count, and that count is zero for shoppers who have not bought this month.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
